title: Digital Wellbeing Redefined: Toward User-Centric Approach for Positive Social Media Engagement
authors: Yixue Zhao, Tianyi Li, Michael Sobolev
text:
In the digital era, the prevalence of social media use, particularly among youth, has raised critical concerns about mental health and digital wellbeing [1,2,3,4]. As we navigate through an increasingly connected world, the impact of digital usage on our psychological and emotional states becomes a crucial area of research [5,1,6,7,8,9]. Current approaches to digital wellbeing have primarily focused on reducing social media use by incorporating friction, limiting screen time, and altering app aesthetics to make it less engaging [10,11,9,12]. However, these methods often overlook the multifaceted nature of social media—a platform that, when used mindfully, can offer significant benefits such as fostering connections, staying informed, and even enhancing mental health via uplifting content [1]. This paradoxical nature of social media necessitates a more nuanced approach to digital wellbeing. Limiting use without considering the context may not only be ineffective but could also provoke counterproductive behaviors, as users often seek a sense of agency and control over their digital experiences [13]. Inspired by positive computing research [14], we propose a paradigm shift towards empowering users for positive social media engagement. This concept of positive engagement encompasses three levels: (1) self-awareness, which involves understanding one’s social media usage and aspirations for improvement; (2) alignment of personal goals with actual digital behaviors; and (3) enhancement of long-term wellbeing. This perspective moves away from punitive measures for unintended behaviors, such as restricting app usage, which can frequently result in feelings of guilt, regret, and dissatisfaction [15].

To capture this perspective, we redefine digital wellbeing as a harmonious alignment between a user’s intentions and their digital behaviors to enhance long-term wellbeing. In line with our definition, we design PauseNow, a P ersonalized, a daptive, use r-centric i N tervention f o r digital w ell-being. PauseNow discerns discrepancies between intended and actual digital usage and offers customized support based on individual preferences. Utilizing the digital nudging and intention-aware recommendations [16,17,18,19,20], PauseNow reminds users of their original intentions when they veer off course, providing them with full autonomy to tailor the intervention to their specific needs. For instance, if PauseNow detects a user’s shift from a focused information search to aimless browsing, a user-defined system behavior will be triggered to help the user re-evaluate their intentions in the app. These user-defined system behaviors are customizable, such as a prompt recalling the original search query, displaying the current time, or showing the user’s daily goals. It aims to foster mindful interactions with digital platforms, countering social media app’s recommendation algorithms that typically aim to maximize screen time.

As the issue of digital wellbeing grows increasingly vital and widespread [21,7,9], its exploration within the Mobile Software Engineering community remains notably limited. Recent efforts [22,23] have begun to explore this new perspective to support conscious social media use through nudging technology, demonstrating initial promise. However, these interventions are currently preliminary and limited in scope, focusing on specific scenarios such as “infinite scroll” and “pull to refresh” in the newsfeeds [22]. This gap has motivated us to outline important considerations in this emerging field, as well as design PauseNow as a reference framework with broader applicability to guide future research. We aim to spark a dialogue on this important topic, harnessing our collective knowledge and expertise in this research forum.
